title: Is AbbVie (ABBV) Undervalued Following Its Oncology Push? - Simply Wall St

Recent price action has been mixed for AbbVie, with the share price up 7.68% over the past 90 days and 24.81% year to date. At the same time, the 1 year total shareholder return of 28.43% and 5 year total shareholder return of 192.43% point to momentum that has been building over a longer horizon as investors react to its oncology deals and immunology pipeline moves. The valuation work now shows which side current numbers lean toward. The narrative fair value of AbbVie at $310 sits above the last close at $286.20, which frames the oncology push inside a wider story about cash generation and concentration risk. According to IamPotato, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who wrote the narrative, the key question is how long the current immunology engine can carry the rest of the portfolio. AbbVie has largely completed one of the most closely watched product transitions in pharmaceuticals. Skyrizi and Rinvoq have more than offset the steep decline in Humira, driving double-digit revenue growth and allowing the company to raise full-year guidance. The near-term picture is strong, but the portfolio is now heavily concentrated on these two immunology assets, and longer-term patent and competitive risks remain. That lens matters for the new oncology collaboration. AbbVie generated $66.0b in annual revenue and $10.3b in net income, yet the narrative points out that a very large share of that engine now leans on Skyrzi and Rinvoq, with oncology deals like Disco Pharmaceuticals and Elahere aiming to widen the base rather than replace it. Valuation work behind the narrative uses a 7.75% discount rate and arrives at a fair value of $310, which implies AbbVie is about 8% undervalued relative to the last close. The same framework labels the stock as undervalued against that estimate, even as the official value score is just 2 out of 6 and the 1 year total shareholder return of 28.43% and 5 year total shareholder return of 192.43% already reflect strong past gains. On the cash flow side, the separate SWS DCF model currently values AbbVie at $422.51 per share, which is about 32.3% above the last close of $286.20. That model projects future free cash flows from the existing portfolio and pipeline, then discounts them back using a required return to translate longer term expectations into a single figure today. Those two valuation anchors, the $310 fair value in the community narrative and the $422.51 output from the SWS DCF model, both sit above the market price but rely on different assumptions about how long Skyrizi and Rinvoq can support earnings, how oncology and neuroscience evolve, and how debt, negative equity and dividend coverage are managed over time. Still, the AbbVie story can change quickly if Skyrizi or Rinvoq face sharper competition than expected or if oncology additions fail to offset pressure elsewhere. title: Could $1,000 a Month in Dividend Stocks Make You Rich by 2040? - The Globe and Mail
content: Reinvested dividends have accounted for more than 30% of the S&P 500’s total return since 1926. At their five-year growth rates, $1,000 a month in Enterprise Products Partners, AbbVie, or Alphabet would grow to roughly $414,000 to $924,000 by 2040. Reaching $1 million in 14 years requires extraordinary returns, so most investors are better off building wealth over decades. Some investors thumb their noses at dividends because they're not interested in income. That's a mistake. Since 1926, more than 30% of the S&P 500's (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) total return has come from reinvesting dividends. Granted, the percentage has been lower in recent years (due to the index's strong growth). However, dividends are an important component of wealth growth. That raises a question, though: Can you become wealthy investing solely in dividend stocks? Let's narrow the question even further. Could investing $1,000 a month in dividend stocks make you rich by 2040? Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Before we can answer that question, we must first address another critical one: How much money does it take to be rich? Different people will respond differently to that question. The Barenaked Ladies tackled the question in 1992. The title of their song "If I Had a Million Dollars" gives away their answer: a cool $1 million. Many Americans might still agree that having $1 million would qualify a person as rich. However, inflation has eroded the buying power of a dollar (or 1 million of them) over the last 34 years. Charles Schwab's (NYSE:SCHW) 2025 Modern Wealth Survey found that a net worth of $2.3 million was the threshold for being wealthy. But to be financially comfortable, the average response was $839,000. Answers varied considerably by region, though. Let's go with The Barenaked Ladies' number for calculation purposes. Let's also use three very different dividend stocks to determine whether investing $1,000 per month could grow to $1 million by 2040. Enterprise Products Partners(NYSE:EPD) ranks among the most attractive ultra-high-yield dividend stocks. The pipeline stock pays a distribution yield of around 6.3%. Enterprise has increased its distribution for 28 consecutive years. It's remarkably resilient, generating strong cash flow even during the financial crisis of 2008 and 2009 and the COVID-19 pandemic. This midstream energy company has delivered a total return compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of roughly 19% over the past five years. What would buying $1,000 per month of Enterprise Products Partners' units (limited partnerships have units rather than shares) be worth after 14 years at that rate? Around $724,000. That's enough to make many Americans feel financially comfortable, but it's still well below our $1 million threshold to be rich. Maybe turning to dividend royalty would get us closer to reaching the goal. AbbVie (NYSE:ABBV) has increased its dividend for an impressive 53 consecutive years, earning it a spot among the Dividend Kings -- a group of stocks with 50 or more consecutive years of dividend growth. The big drugmaker has successfully navigated a patent cliff and markets multiple blockbuster drugs. AbbVie's forward dividend yield is slightly north of 2.5%, which is lower than historical levels primarily because the pharma stock has performed well. As a result, AbbVie's total return CAGR over the last five years is around 22%. If you bought $1,000 of the stock each month through 2040, you'd have almost $924,000 at that growth rate. We wouldn't quite reach the $1 million mark, but we'd be closer with AbbVie than with Enterprise Products Partners. What if we focused more on growth than dividends? Google parent Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG)(NASDAQ:GOOGL) pays a minuscule dividend yield of 0.33%. However, the company is a leader in several key technologies shaping the future, including artificial intelligence (AI), cloud services, driverless cars, and quantum computing. You might think all of this would be enough to vault Alphabet well past Enterprise Products Partners and AbbVie. However, that's not the case. Over the last five years, Alphabet's total return CAGR was around 12% -- a respectable but not jaw-dropping number. Investing $1,000 per month in the stock through 2040 at this CAGR would give you less than $414,000 at the end of the 14 years. So what's the answer to our initial question? Investing $1,000 a month in dividend stocks could make you rich by 2040 (with "rich" defined as $1 million), but you would need to find stocks that deliver extraordinarily high total returns. That's easier said than done. None of the three stocks we evaluated would have achieved the goal. Note, too, that the calculations above assumed that Enterprise Products Partners, AbbVie, and Alphabet would continue to grow at the same rate as they have over the past five years. That may or may not be the case. There's another approach, though, that could be better for most investors. Don't worry about becoming rich in 14 years; focus on growing your wealth over the long term -- multiple decades. With a diversified portfolio of solid dividend stocks, that goal should be attainable. The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.
